Figure methods and captions

The conceptual framework is Figure 1. The empirical figures below follow the order used in the manuscript. Method summaries are working text and are kept separate from the publication-ready captions.

Figure 2 — Holocene climate change and fire

Method summary. Adjacent 1,000-year changes in spring temperature, winter temperature, summer precipitation, and winter precipitation were evaluated at ten 100-year phases and standardized by the corresponding standard deviations among the 618 legacy CCA calibration plots. The three MORA lake trajectories were averaged before MORA and NOCA received equal regional weight. A variable qualified when its absolute median regional change reached 50% of its maximum and at least eight phases supported its direction; any qualifying variable defined climate change. High-fire periods were classified independently from accepted charcoal-event frequencies normalized within core and aggregated by site, using a threshold of the site median plus 1.4826 × MAD. Anthropocene climate contrasts compare 1979–1989 with six season-years Y−5 through Y for each plot, where Y is the selected adult resurvey year. Midpoint intervals run from 1984 to Y−2.5: 27.5–32.5 years at MORA and 27.5–28.5 years at NOCA.

Figure 2. Holocene climate change and fire.

Publication-ready caption. Figure 2. Holocene climate-change eras and high-fire evidence at Mount Rainier (MORA) and North Cascades (NOCA). A. Signed 1,000-year changes in the four CCA climate variables, standardized by their pooled legacy-calibration standard deviations and summarized with equal weight for MORA and NOCA. Points mark variables meeting both the variable-specific magnitude threshold and the eight-of-ten phase-direction criterion. Background bands identify climate-change (CC) and climate-stability (S) eras; arrows show the direction of time, and CC1a–CC1c annotations describe the retained climate directions within CC1. Brackets at the older margin show the variable-specific standardized stability ranges. The inset compares the maximum-absolute Holocene regional median after ten-offset aggregation with median Anthropocene plot-level rates in physical units per century. The Anthropocene entries are annualized short-window contrasts: MORA compares 1979–1989 with each plot’s adult-year window Y−5 through Y over 27.5–32.5 midpoint years; NOCA uses the same rule over 27.5–28.5 midpoint years. The MORA precipitation contrast should be interpreted with the documented possible post-2010 CHELSA inhomogeneity. B. Site-specific charcoal event-frequency ratios relative to the robust high-fire threshold. The dashed line denotes a ratio of 1; red segments and points identify dates classified as high fire. Ages are calibrated years before present (cal BP; present = 1950).

Figure 3 — Observed and climate-predicted CCA trajectories

Method summary. A common canonical correspondence analysis (CCA) was fit to 13 retained taxa and four seasonal climate constraints in 618 legacy plots. Observed communities were represented by weighted-average (WA) scores and climate-predicted communities by linear-combination (LC) scores in the unchanged CCA1–CCA2, scaling-1 (scaling = "sites"), Hill-off geometry. Holocene positions are MORA and NOCA centroids within each frozen CC1–S4 era; Anthropocene positions are site means of the same 330 MORA and 275 NOCA valid paired plots at both legacy and resurvey dates, for both WA and LC. MORA uses the latest adult visit and its matching seedlings; modern climate uses Y−5 through Y for each selected adult survey year Y. All-zero retained-taxon rows are excluded from both sides of these comparisons. Climate bars quantify each constraint’s unique marginal loss of constrained inertia, whereas species bars partition constrained inertia among taxa.

Figure 3. Observed and climate-predicted CCA trajectories.

Publication-ready caption. Figure 3. Observed and climate-predicted forest community trajectories in the common CCA space. A. Observed WA and climate-predicted LC trajectories for MORA and NOCA. Holocene paths connect site-level centroids chronologically from CC1 through S4; Anthropocene arrows connect legacy and resurvey means from identical valid pairs at both dates (330 MORA, 275 NOCA). Predicted paths and annotations are shown with reduced opacity. The grey points are legacy calibration plots; the panel is cropped to the trajectories; calibration plots outside the displayed extent remain in the model. B. CCA biplot showing the four climate vectors and species scores; all taxa are plotted, while names are shown only for species vectors at least 25% as long as the longest species vector. C. Unique marginal effect of each climate constraint, expressed as a percentage of total constrained inertia. These values are not additive because the constraints share explanatory variation. D. Taxon-specific partition of constrained inertia; shading indicates occurrence in the 618 calibration plots.

Figure 4 — Community tracking comparison

Method summary. At each endpoint, climate–community offset was the distance between predicted LC and observed WA scores. Lag per century was the change in this offset divided by elapsed time. Observed and predicted turnover were WA and LC displacement rates, respectively; their ratio was observed/predicted turnover, and their angle measured directional agreement. Holocene nonlinear metrics were calculated for every site × age draw × offset × interval realization before draws were summarized within offsets and all ten offsets were summarized on the reporting grid. Anthropocene metrics were calculated for paired legacy–resurvey plots.

Figure 4. Community tracking comparison.

Publication-ready caption. Figure 4. Comparison of climate–community tracking during the Holocene and Anthropocene at MORA and NOCA. A–C. Lag per century, tracking ratio (observed/predicted), and angle between observed and predicted turnover vectors. Upper panels compare Holocene site-dates with Anthropocene plot pairs; lower panels divide Holocene site-dates between climate change and climate stability and by high-fire evidence. Boxes have fixed physical widths and show descriptive distributions; annotations report medians and valid sample sizes. Neutral and red outlines distinguish no-fire/unburned and high-fire/burned groups. The two burned MORA plot pairs are excluded from this comparison and retained in its scope audit. D. Tracking ratio versus turnover angle for all 589 direction-valid observations. Circles and triangles identify MORA and NOCA, red outlines identify fire evidence, and fill represents signed lag. Labelled points are macro-era, climate/fire, and NOCA burn-status medians. Reference lines mark a tracking ratio of 1 and an angle of 90°. The 151 Anthropocene plots with stationary observed composition have undefined angles and are reported separately in the panel.

Figure 5 — Target-alignment discrepancies

Method summary. For every plot pair and Holocene age-draw × offset × interval realization, predicted and observed movements were compared separately with 13 taxon directions and four unscaled climate biplot arrows. For each taxon, the predicted cosine uses the vector from the initial LC position to the fixed taxon score, whereas the observed cosine uses the vector from the initial WA position to that score. The target-alignment discrepancy was calculated within each unit as cos(predicted movement, target) - cos(observed movement, target) before any aggregation. Near-zero or non-finite movement or target vectors were assigned NA. Holocene draws were summarized within offsets, then across all ten offsets at each site-date, before climate-state and high-fire grouping; Anthropocene units were grouped by site and burned status.

Figure 5. Climate and taxon target-alignment discrepancies.

Publication-ready caption. Figure 5. Differences between predicted and observed community-change alignment with climate and taxon directions. A. Median target-alignment discrepancies for the four CCA climate vectors. B. Median target-alignment discrepancies for the 13 retained taxa. Columns show Holocene climate change and climate stability with or without high-fire evidence, followed by burned and unburned Anthropocene plots; MORA and NOCA are shown in separate facets. Red group text identifies high-fire or burned groups. Cell color is the median predicted-minus-observed cosine difference among valid measurement units. For taxa, predicted and observed cosines use their own initial LC and WA origins, respectively, toward the same fixed species score; climate cosines use the corresponding common biplot arrow. Zero indicates equal target-specific cosines, not agreement between the complete movement vectors. Positive values indicate stronger predicted target alignment, including cases where predicted movement is merely less strongly opposed to the target; negative values indicate stronger observed target alignment. Magnitude describes the strength of this target-specific discrepancy; it does not measure taxon dominance, statistical significance, or causation.
